parts.title: How Competition Within and Between Species Shapes Where Three Top Predators Live Together
parts.abstract:
ABSTRACT

To protect top predators and look after the places they live, we need to know where their populations are and which kinds of places they choose. Earlier studies have shown that the features of the land and the amount of food affect these choices. But they have often overlooked something else: competition, both between animals of the same species and between different species.

We used 6 years (2014–2019) of continuous data from infrared camera traps, which are motion-triggered cameras that take pictures automatically, in the Hunchun region of China. With them, we tracked how the numbers of three species living side by side changed: Amur tigers (Panthera tigris altaica), Amur leopards (P. pardus orientalis) and Asiatic black bears (Ursus thibetanus). We also used a statistical method called Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) to describe which places each of the three species chose.

Over this period, the number of Amur tigers per area rose by a statistically significant amount (p = 0.05), and so did the number of Amur leopards (p = 0.035). A result is called statistically significant when, if there were really no change, a trend this strong would rarely appear by chance alone. For Asiatic black bears, the change was not significant (p = 0.86), so we could not show a change for them. As the populations recovered, each of the three top predators affected where the other species lived in its own way.

Our results also show that where top predators choose to live comes from several things working together: competition within and between species, the features of the land, and how much prey is available. In particular, the number of Amur tigers and leopards in an area affected where tigers and leopards themselves went. The numbers of tigers and leopards also affected where Asiatic black bears went.

For this reason, we believe conservation should move beyond simply bringing back prey animals. It should meet the basic habitat needs of meat-eating animals as a whole, and manage competition for space. This includes carefully planned efforts to guide key species to new areas, so that their populations can keep growing in a lasting way.
parts.introduction_first:
Ecologists have long wanted to understand how species that need similar things can live in the same place (Di Bitetti et al. 2010; Ramesh et al. 2012; Li et al. 2024). The idea of an ecological niche says that each species has its own role in an ecosystem, such as what it eats, where it lives and when it is active. The more closely two species fill the same role, the harder it is for them to live together. So the number and variety of species that can share a community are limited by how alike their roles are (Jaksic and Marone 2007; Di Bitetti et al. 2010).

Top predators matter here too. When a community is dominated by meat-eating top predators, they shape the lives of the animals below them in the food chain. This is called a top-down effect. It helps keep the ecosystem in balance, both through the ways species affect one another and through trophic cascades, which are chains of knock-on effects that spread down the food chain (Hunter and Price 1992; Elmhagen et al. 2010; Colman et al. 2014). Top predators also affect which species live in a community and how many of each there are (Paine 1980, Terborgh et al. 2001; Dorresteijn et al. 2015).

Human activity makes things harder. When people disturb the land and break natural habitat into small, separate patches, competition between species grows stronger (Symes et al. 2018; Kadoya et al. 2022; Carvalho Jr. et al. 2025; Jin et al. 2025). As populations grow, more animals end up in the same area. This makes competition stronger both within a species and between different species. In response, animals come to put first the places that give them the best chance of surviving and raising young (Stamps and Krishnan 1995; Fedriani et al. 1999; Andheria et al. 2007; Ramesh et al. 2012; Sugimoto et al. 2016).
parts.conclusion:
5

Conclusion

We carefully studied 6 years of infrared camera trap data from the Hunchun region. Over that time, the populations of Amur tigers and Amur leopards recovered significantly, while the number of Asiatic black bears stayed fairly steady. Even with this recovery, all three species were growing more slowly than before. This suggests that competition within each species has become stronger in the limited habitat.

Our study also shows that top predators are shaped by more than the usual factors, such as the features of the land and the amount of prey. Their recovery and where they live depend strongly on competition within and between species. In particular, the number of tigers and leopards in an area has a significant effect on where tigers and leopards themselves choose to go. Where Asiatic black bears go is clearly shaped by the numbers of these two big cats.

These findings offer new insights that can guide future efforts to protect large meat-eating animals that live side by side in Northeast China. It is essential to look at changes in populations together with the pressure of competition within and between species, especially because each species needs different things from its habitat. For this reason, conservation should move beyond simply bringing back prey animals. It should meet the basic habitat needs of meat-eating animals as a whole. To deal with the pressure of competition, we recommend carefully planned efforts to guide key species to new areas, so that the populations of the Amur tiger, the Amur leopard and the Asiatic black bear can keep growing in a lasting way.
parts.introduction_rest:
Three top predators live side by side across northeast China and the Russian Far East: the Amur tiger (Panthera tigris altaica), the Amur leopard (P. pardus orientalis) and the Asiatic black bear (Ursus thibetanus) (Robert Steinmetz et al. 2013, Seryodkin et al. 2018). The IUCN Red List is a worldwide list that rates how close each species is to dying out. On that list, the Amur tiger is Endangered, the Amur leopard is Critically Endangered and the Asiatic black bear is Vulnerable (Uphyrkina 2002, Dinerstein et al. 2007, Garshelis and Steinmetz 2020).

These animals are keystone meat-eaters. Like a keystone that holds up an arch, they help keep ecosystems stable, both in how they are built and in how they work. They do this by keeping plant-eating animals in check and by holding back the strongest competitors (Ripple et al. 2014; She et al. 2022).

In the past, these predators became much fewer in China. The main reasons were that people took away their habitat and ate up their prey, as human pressure on the land grew (Yu et al. 2009; Jiang et al. 2015; Wan et al. 2019). Fortunately, recent conservation work has helped protect and restore the places where wildlife lives. This work includes the Grain-for-Green Program, which turns farmland back into forest, the National Natural Forest Protection Project, and the creation of national parks (Jiang et al. 2017; Wang et al. 2023). As these populations recover, we now have a rare chance to watch how the animals change the places they choose to live.

Even though the populations are recovering, very few studies have looked at how population growth and the choice of habitat are linked in Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears. Most earlier research has focused on the features of the land and on how much prey is available. It has often overlooked competition within and between species, which grows stronger as more animals crowd into the same area. On top of that, such studies usually use data collected over only a short time. This makes it hard to see how animals choose their habitat while their numbers rise and fall (McLoughlin et al. 2010).

To fill these gaps, we used 6 years (2014–2019) of continuous data from infrared camera traps in Hunchun, China. With them, we studied how the populations of these three predators changed and which places they chose. We tested two ideas, or hypotheses. First, we expected that as conservation efforts grew stronger, wildlife populations would keep rising, and that the presence of top predators would shape where the other species lived across the landscape. Second, we expected that, besides the features of the land and the amount of prey, competition within and between species would have a significant effect on where these three top predators living side by side choose to go.
parts.methods:
2

Methods

2.1

Where We Did the Study

We carried out this study in Hunchun, in Jilin Province in northeastern China. The site used to be part of the Hunchun National Nature Reserve for Amur Tigers, which lies between 130°14′08″ and 131°14′44″ east and between 42°24′40″ and 43°28′00″ north (Li et al. 2008). The land is mostly low mountains in the Laoyeling Mountains, part of the larger Changbai Mountain range. Heights range from 5 m to 1477 m above sea level. Because the area is close to the Sea of Japan, the average temperature over a year is 5.65°C, and on average 617.9 mm of rain and snow falls each year. The plants here follow a clear yearly cycle: a growing season from May to October and a non-growing season from November to April (Li et al. 2008; Liu et al. 2021; Wen et al. 2024).

The study area borders Russia's Land of the Leopard National Park in Primorsky Krai. Over time, more and more Amur tigers and leopards have crossed the border between the two countries, and their populations have been recovering (Gu et al. 2018). The region is an important home for Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears (Vitkalova et al. 2018). It is also one of the most important wildlife corridors that cross the border between China and Russia, and it will matter for future efforts to protect wildlife on both sides (Gu et al. 2018) (Figure 1).

FIGURE 1

Map of where the 60 camera traps were placed in the study area. The cameras were set up from January 2014 to December 2019.

The area is rich in wildlife. The main animals are the Amur tiger, the Amur leopard, the Asiatic black bear, the sika deer (Cervus nippon), the roe deer (Capreolus pygargus), the wild boar (Sus scrofa), the red fox (Vulpes vulpes), the Eurasian badger (Meles meles) and the raccoon dog (Nyctereutes procyonoides). Most of the forest is oak forest or larch forest, with mixed forests, spruce forests, birch forests and Korean pine forests as well. There are also a few scattered villages. As the weather warms through the seasons, local people grow crops, graze cattle and gather wild vegetables and mushrooms in certain parts of the study area.

2.2

How We Used the Camera Traps

From 2014 to 2019, we used infrared camera traps to collect information about the wildlife. Our main focus was on three top predators and on hoofed animals such as deer and boar. We divided the study area into squares of 3.2 × 3.2 km and placed a pair of cameras in each square, giving 60 camera stations in total. We chose this spacing based on the size of the area that hoofed animals normally roam over, called their home range (Ofstad et al. 2016). It also matches the long-term camera plan that has been used in this region for many years (Qi et al. 2021; She et al. 2022). Spacing the cameras this way covers the home ranges of hoofed animals and other small animals, while also reducing spatial autocorrelation, which is the problem of cameras close together recording almost the same things (Legendre 1993; Silveira et al. 2003; Qi et al. 2021).

When choosing where to put the cameras, we placed them where mammals are likely to pass, such as ridges, valleys, trails, forest roads and places animals can reach water. This gave us the best chance of catching wildlife on camera (Wang et al. 2016; She et al. 2022). At each station, one camera stood on each side of the trail, both facing the trail. Each camera was fixed to a tree trunk about 40–80 cm above the ground and 3–5 m from the spot it was meant to watch (Jacobs and Ausband 2018). This setup let us photograph Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears, and also hoofed animals and other small mammals such as foxes, badgers, yellow-throated martens and hares. Every 3 months, we checked and looked after the cameras. We cleared anything blocking the camera's view, replaced cameras that were missing or broken, copied the pictures and changed the batteries.

To handle the camera pictures, we first picked out every image or video that showed animals or people. We then identified and sorted each one by species or by human disturbance, and noted the time and date it was taken. To avoid counting the same animal twice, we treated photos of the same species taken less than 0.5 hours apart as one event, and photos taken more than 0.5 hours apart as separate, valid events (O'Brien et al. 2003).

2.3

How the Numbers of the Three Top Predators Changed, and Where They Lived

Mammals at different levels of the food chain spread out over the land in different ways. Species higher up the food chain, or those that travel more widely, may be photographed by several cameras (She et al. 2024). This means the raw camera counts can be misleading. To correct for this and make our analysis more reliable, we used a method called the Random Encounter Model. It turns the separate photos into a more trustworthy estimate of how many animals of each species there are (Rowcliffe et al. 2008; She et al. 2024). The formula is:

D = y / (t × vi × r² × θ)

Here, D is the number of animals of a species per area. The letter y is the number of separate photos of that species per unit of time, and t is the length of time in days. The letter vi is how fast species i moves each day (Table S2), r is the distance from the camera that it can watch, and θ is the angle the camera can see.

First, we used boxplots, a type of chart that shows the middle and spread of a set of values, to show the relative density of six target species in the study area: Amur tigers, Amur leopards, Asiatic black bears, roe deer, wild boar and sika deer. We then used a generalized additive model (GAM), a statistical method that can follow curved trends over time, to show how their relative density changed from year to year between 2014 and 2019.

Next, we took Amur tigers as an example. We sorted the camera stations into two groups: stations where Amur tigers were present and stations where they were absent. We then compared how the numbers of the other species (not counting Amur tigers) changed at these two kinds of stations from 2014 to 2019. We did exactly the same for Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears.

2.4

Modeling Which Places the Three Top Predators Chose

We downloaded a digital elevation model, a map of land height made of squares 30 m across, from the geospatial data cloud (https://www.gscloud.cn). Maps of vegetation type, villages, farmland, rivers and roads came from the National Geographic Information Resource Catalog Service System (http://www.webmap.cn). Using the mapping software ArcGIS 10.8.2, we worked out the slope (how steep the ground is) and the aspect (which direction a slope faces) from the height map. We then used a tool called Multivalue Extraction to Points to read off the height, slope and aspect at each camera spot. Finally, we used a tool called Nearest Neighbor Analysis to measure how far each camera spot was from villages, farmland, rivers, roads and particular types of forest, for use in our analysis.

First, we standardized the measurements, which means putting them all on the same scale so that they could be compared fairly (Jiang et al. 2010). Some measurements tend to rise and fall together, and using both can confuse a model. To find such pairs, we used the Pearson correlation test, which gives a number showing how closely two measurements move together. We ran it on height, slope, aspect and the distances to rivers, farmland, villages, roads and different forest types, using the "corSelect" function in the statistics program R. When the correlation was greater than 0.7, we treated the two measurements as strongly linked and removed one of them before building the model (Ramsay et al. 2003; Dormann et al. 2013; Li et al. 2017).

We then used Generalized Linear Mixed Models (GLMMs) to build the best model of what affects where Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears choose to live. For the Amur tiger model, the thing we were trying to explain was whether Amur tigers were present or absent at a spot. The things we used to explain it were the relative density of Amur tigers in the year before (Nt−1), and the numbers of Amur leopards, Asiatic black bears, roe deer, wild boar and sika deer, human disturbance, and the different land features in the same year (Nt). Together, these let us measure the overall effects of competition, prey and the features of the land. We also included the year as a random effect. This lets the model allow for the fact that tigers' choices may shift from one year to the next, without treating each year as a separate factor.

We fitted the GLMMs with the R package "YawMMF". We used the "dredge" function in the "MuMIn" package to try every possible combination of the factors in the model. We then compared the models using the Akaike Information Criterion adjusted for small samples (AICc), a score that rewards a model for fitting the data well but penalizes it for being too complicated. We kept every model whose score was within 2 points of the best one (△AICc < 2), worked out the Akaike weight (ωi) of each model, which shows how much support each model has compared with the others, and chose the model with the lowest score (Guthery et al. 2003; Brewer et al. 2016).

For the best model, we used the function r.squaredGLMM() to calculate two kinds of R², which show how much of the variation in the data a model explains. The marginal R² (R²m) counts only the factors we measured, while the conditional R² (R²c) also includes the year-to-year differences (Zhang et al. 2020; Lai 2023). We used the "confint()" function to calculate confidence intervals for each factor in the model, which are ranges that show how uncertain each estimate is. We built the models for Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears in the same way as for Amur tigers, and we did all of this analysis in R (R Core Team 2024).
parts.results:
3

Results

3.1

How the Numbers of the Three Top Predators Changed, and Where They Lived

From January 2014 to December 2019, our camera traps in the study area ran for a total of 120,085 days (Table A1). Over those years, the cameras recorded Amur tigers 453 times, Amur leopards 341 times and Asiatic black bears 94 times.

We first looked at how the number of each animal per area changed from 2014 to 2019. We did this for the three top predators and for the hoofed animals that eat plants, such as deer and boar. Amur leopards (p = 0.035), roe deer (p < 0.01), wild boars (p < 0.01) and sika deer (p < 0.01) all showed statistically significant growth. Amur tigers also grew from 2016 to 2019 (p = 0.05). For Asiatic black bears, the change was not significant (p = 0.86; Figure 2).

FIGURE 2

How the number of Amur tigers, Amur leopards, Asiatic black bears and other species living side by side changed from 2014 to 2019. The horizontal axis shows the year, and the vertical axis shows the number of each species per area, averaged for each year. The box plots show how the estimates for each year were spread out. The dashed line is a smooth curve fitted to the yearly values (a method called a GAM), and the shaded band shows the 95% confidence interval, the range in which the true trend is likely to lie.

Next, we used the records of Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears to sort the camera trap stations into two groups. At "presence" stations, the species had been recorded. At "absence" stations, it had not. This let us see how the numbers of the three top predators changed in each kind of place.

At stations where Amur tigers were absent, the number of Amur leopards per area rose significantly (p < 0.01). At stations where Amur tigers were present, the change for Asiatic black bears was not significant (p = 0.45). The other way round, at tiger presence stations, the number of Asiatic black bears per area rose significantly (p = 0.029), while the change for Amur leopards was not significant (p = 0.2) (Figure 3a,b).

We also looked at the hoofed prey animals and at human activity. For roe deer (p0 < 0.01, p1 < 0.01) and wild boar (p0 < 0.01, p1 = 0.032), the results showed a significant relationship. Here p0 stands for the absence stations and p1 for the presence stations. Sika deer showed a significant rise at tiger absence stations (p = 0.01), but no clear change at tiger presence stations (p = 0.91). Human activity did not differ significantly between the two kinds of station (p0 = 0.20, p1 = 0.96) (Figure S1).

FIGURE 3

How the numbers of two other top predators changed from 2014 to 2019 at stations where Amur tigers were absent ("0") and present ("1"). The horizontal axis shows the year, and the vertical axis shows the number of each species per area, averaged for each year. The box plots show how the estimates for each year were spread out. The dashed line is a smooth curve fitted to the yearly values (a GAM), and the shaded band shows the 95% confidence interval.

At stations where Amur leopards were absent, the number of Amur tigers per area rose significantly (p = 0.01). The change for Asiatic black bears was not significant (p = 0.55). At leopard presence stations, the changes for both Amur tigers (p = 0.068) and Asiatic black bears (p = 0.096) were not significant (Figure 3c,d).

The hoofed prey animals showed the same pattern as before. Roe deer (p0 < 0.01, p1 < 0.01) and wild boar (p0 < 0.01, p1 < 0.01) had significant relationships with the two kinds of station. Sika deer rose significantly at leopard absence stations (p = 0.022), but the change was not significant at leopard presence stations (p = 0.086). Human activity did not differ significantly between the two kinds of station (p0 = 0.90, p1 = 0.62) (Figure S2).

Finally, we looked at the stations where Asiatic black bears were present or absent. The number of Amur tigers per area rose significantly at both kinds of station (p = 0.01). The number of Amur leopards per area also rose significantly, both at absence stations (p0 = 0.01) and at presence stations (p1 = 0.049) (Figure 3e,f).

The hoofed prey animals showed significant relationships at both kinds of station. These were roe deer (p0 < 0.01, p1 < 0.01), sika deer (p0 = 0.027, p1 = 0.021) and wild boar (p0 < 0.01, p1 = 0.019). Human activity did not differ significantly between the two kinds of station (p0 = 0.44, p1 = 0.69) (Figure S3).

3.2

Which Places the Three Top Predators Chose, and How Competition Within and Between Species Affected This

For each species, we built several possible models of where it chose to live. Each model is a different combination of factors, such as height above sea level, the number of other animals nearby, and distance to rivers or forests. We then compared them to find the best one. Amur tigers had 5 models, Amur leopards had 2 and Asiatic black bears had 4 (Table S3).

For Amur tigers, the best model was a type called a GLMM. It showed that tigers avoided higher ground (p = 0.015), so they tended to be found in lower areas. Tigers also tended to avoid places with more wild boar (p = 0.056).

Tigers were more likely to be present where there were more Amur tigers in the year before (p = 0.015), more roe deer (p = 0.012) and more human activity (p = 0.006). They were also more likely to be present closer to farmland (p = 0.01). For sika deer, however, tigers showed no clear preference, whether the deer were present or absent (p = 0.155, 95% confidence interval = −0.093 to 0.841).

We also measured how much of the variation in where tigers went each part of the model explained. The part explained by the factors we measured (R²m) was 0.423. The part explained by the factors plus the year (R²c) was 0.525. The year on its own explained 0.102. This shows that the places tigers chose did not change much from year to year.

For Amur leopards, the GLMM showed that leopards were significantly more likely to be present where there were more Amur leopards in the year before (p = 0.012), more black bears (p = 0.034), more distance to rivers (p = 0.003) and more larch trees (p = 0.001). They were significantly less likely to be present higher up (p = 0.004) and farther from Korean pines (p = 0.012). Roe deer density showed no clear preference (p = 0.059, 95% confidence interval = −0.015 to 0.567).

In the leopard model, R²m and R²c were both 0.176. The year added nothing to the explanation, which shows that the places leopards chose did not change much from year to year.

For Asiatic black bears, the best model showed that bears were more likely to be present where there were more Amur tigers (p ≤ 0.001) and more Amur leopards (p = 0.009). They were also more likely to be present farther from oak forests (p ≤ 0.001) and less likely to be present farther from national highways (p = 0.002).

The direction a slope faced (p = 0.082, 95% confidence interval = −0.036 to 0.700) and the distance to birch forests (p = 0.106, 95% confidence interval = −0.818 to 0.062) showed no clear preference. In the black bear model, R²m was 0.157 and R²c was 0.160. The year on its own explained only 0.003 (Table 1). This shows that the places black bears chose did not change much from year to year.

parts.discussion:
4

Discussion

4.1

How the Numbers of Three Top Predators Changed, and Where They Lived

Our results confirm that, apart from the slow growth of the Asiatic black bear population, the numbers of Amur leopards, roe deer, wild boar and sika deer rose by a statistically significant amount. The number of Amur tigers also rose (Figure 2). These findings agree with earlier research on how Amur tiger and leopard populations have been changing (Jiang et al. 2017; Qi et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2023).

Our research also shows that whether Amur tigers, Amur leopards or Asiatic black bears are present in an area leads to different patterns in where the other species live. All three are top predators, but they do not play exactly the same part in keeping the ecosystem in balance. Where they live side by side, Amur tigers dominated the competition between species, while Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears were the weaker competitors (Harihar et al. 2011; Hojnowski et al. 2012). As a result, the number of Amur leopards per area did not rise significantly in places where Amur tigers were present, while Amur leopards had very little effect on Amur tigers.

What the animals eat tells part of the story. Studies of their diets show that Amur tigers mainly prefer wild boar and sika deer, while Amur leopards prefer sika deer and roe deer (Gu et al. 2018; Yang et al. 2018). Yet in areas where Amur leopards were present, the number of sika deer per area rose more slowly, while the numbers of roe deer and wild boar kept growing as before.

At the same time, the number of Asiatic black bears per area rose at sites where Amur tigers and leopards were present. This is likely because Asiatic black bears scavenge, which means they feed on the remains of animals killed by other hunters. Here they scavenge at the spots where tigers and leopards have killed prey, so they can get food (Seryodkin et al. 2018). Asiatic black bears are also top predators, but their part in keeping the ecosystem in balance seems to be weaker than that of Amur tigers and Amur leopards.

4.2

Where the Three Top Predators Live When They Share the Same Land and Compete Within and Between Species

How many prey animals there are, and where they live, strongly affects which places top predators choose (Silveira et al. 2003). The quality of the habitat, how much food and other resources are available, and competition within and between species also play a part (Fretwell and Lucas 1969; Rosenzweig 1981; Karanth et al. 2004; Santora et al. 2011).

Amur tigers, Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears are territorial, which means each animal keeps a fairly fixed home range, an area it defends as its own. For animals like this, it is important to consider how many members of their own species live in an area when we study where they choose to live (O'Neil et al. 2019). This matters especially when populations rise and fall. As the number of animals in an area shifts, the way a species responds to different features of the land in a habitat model can change, and this changes what the model shows (O'Neil et al. 2019).

Our results show that the number of Amur tigers and leopards per area had a significant effect on where they chose to live. This likely happens because, as more animals of the same species crowd into an area, more individuals end up without a home range of their own. The animals that already own a territory may then defend it more strongly, using particular places more to protect their territory. So, to protect these territorial species, it is crucial to understand the pressure on space that comes from growing populations, and the territorial behaviour animals use to secure their places.

Earlier research shows that when a population becomes crowded and competition grows, territorial species make more use of secondary habitats, meaning places that are less suitable than their best ones (Morris 1994). For example, O'Neil used a method called Resource Selection Probability Functions (RSPF), which compares how often animals use each kind of place with how common that kind of place is. O'Neil showed that as the number of wolves per area rose, established packs put high-quality habitat first, which pushed other wolves into lower-quality habitat.

In line with this, our GLMM analysis showed that the number of Amur tigers and Amur leopards per area had a significant effect on where they chose to live, but this was not the case for Asiatic black bears. We carried out this study in a region on the border between China and Russia, where many Amur tigers and Amur leopards move back and forth across the border. For these territorial big cats, the link between the number of their own species in an area and where they choose to live may come from competition between animals that already own a territory and "floaters", which are animals without a territory.

The Asiatic black bear population, by contrast, has shown no significant change in its numbers, or no clear growth, in recent years. As a result, where Asiatic black bears chose to live was more strongly affected by the presence of Amur tigers and Amur leopards. Although Asiatic black bears eat both plants and animals, they get food by scavenging the remains of animals killed by Amur tigers and leopards. This scavenging often happens some time after the kill (Seryodkin et al. 2018).

Earlier studies of what these predators eat found that roe deer, wild boar and sika deer are the main prey of Amur tigers and leopards. Tigers strongly prefer wild boar, followed by sika deer and then roe deer, while leopards prefer roe deer and avoid wild boar (Yang et al. 2018). However, our model found a significant positive link only between the presence of Amur tigers and the number of roe deer per area. In other words, where there were more roe deer, tigers were more likely to be present. When we included the year as a random factor, meaning we allowed for differences between years, this positive link between tigers and roe deer was significant, while the links with sika deer and wild boar were not significant.

We also found a significant positive link between the presence of Amur tigers and both human disturbance and closeness to farmland. This suggests that as the number of tigers per area grows, conflict between people and tigers could get worse. It shows that managers need to use strategies that keep people and tigers apart in space and time, so that such conflicts can be reduced (Cheng et al. 2024).

We also found a significant link between Amur leopards and Asiatic black bears in the places they chose. This may be because Amur leopards and tigers use very different parts of the landscape, while Asiatic black bears roam over a wide area. Together, this means leopards and bears overlap more in the space they use.

Overall, our study shows that competition within a species has a significant effect on where Amur tigers and leopards choose to live, and that the presence of tigers and leopards also has a significant effect on where Asiatic black bears go.
